meta.title: Why Your New Car Is Basically a Giant Phone (And Why That's Dangerous)
meta.working_title: It's Illegal to Use Your Phone While Driving. So Why Is There One in Your Dashboard?
meta.device: Running 'EYES OFF ROAD' meter in the top-left corner: metres driven blind per task, ticking up whenever a screen is touched. Recurring symbol: Dave's nodding-dog dashboard toy, which nods happily at buttons and shakes its head at screens.
meta.style: Consumer-tech rant explainer in the house 2D style (Gumball/t-shirt rig), painterly plates: a rainy M62 motorway at dusk seen through a windscreen, a 2005 estate-car dashboard full of chunky buttons, a modern glowing tablet dashboard, a Swedish test track, a car-design studio, a German boardroom, a glossy motor-show stand, a monthly-bill kitchen table, a scrapyard, a Rome launch stage, a Porsche-style workshop. Real people stylised, no likeness, no real logos (brand names as text only). SFX under VO (rain, wipers, indicator ticks, button clicks, touchscreen blips, horns), music at combine.
meta.source: YouTube reference (TopCars TV, 'STOP turning Cars into Phones', 10:56) used as research only; facts checked against Vi Bilägare, Autocar/Paul Tan (VW Mindt), Fortune/Motor1 (Mercedes), Tesla/Consumer Reports (3G), Porsche newsroom (2025 results), The Week/TNW (Ferrari Luce), The Drive/Motor1 (Mission S). Original script in our own words, en-GB.

shots.vo: Picture this. A wet Tuesday on the M62. Seventy miles an hour, lorries throwing spray, and your windscreen starts to steam up.
shots.visual: Dusk motorway in rain, camera rides behind the windscreen of Dave's car; wipers thrash; red tail-lights smear; fog creeps across the glass.
shots.anim: Wipers sweep, condensation spreads from the edges.

shots.vo: In a car from 2005, you don't even look down. Your hand finds the big chunky button by feel. Click. Done. Eyes never leave the road.
shots.visual: Old estate dashboard: Dave's hand slides to a fat demist button without looking; nodding dog nods; the glass clears.
shots.anim: Button press with a satisfying click; fog wipes away.

shots.vo: Now try it in a brand-new car. Wake the screen. Find the climate menu. Swipe. Hunt for a demist icon the size of a Tic Tac. Then hit a pothole and jab the wrong thing.
shots.visual: Modern glowing tablet dash: Dave's finger hovers, menus slide, a tiny icon; a bump jolts and the finger lands on 'Heated steering wheel'; the EYES OFF ROAD meter starts ticking.
shots.anim: Menus slide, pothole jolt, wrong icon flashes, meter ticks up.

shots.vo: Here's the funny bit. Holding your phone at the wheel can cost you six points and a two-hundred-pound fine. But a carmaker bolting a fifteen-inch tablet to your dashboard? Apparently that's fine.
shots.visual: Split: a police officer writes a ticket for a phone; on the right a salesman proudly unveils a giant screen in a showroom; nodding dog shakes its head.
shots.anim: Ticket rips off the pad; the screen unveiling gets sparkles.

shots.visual: Title card: a car dashboard morphing into a giant phone, with a home bar where the speedo was.
shots.onscreen: YOUR CAR IS A PHONE NOW
shots.anim: Dashboard melts into a phone; title stamps.

acts.name: How the tablet ate the dashboard

shots.vo: So how did we get here? Rewind to 2012. Tesla launches the Model S with a seventeen-inch touchscreen in the middle of the dash, and the world loses its mind.
shots.visual: A bright launch stage in 2012; a sleek saloon rolls out; the giant portrait screen glows; a crowd of phones film it.
shots.anim: Car rolls in, screen powers on with a glow, flashbulbs pop.

shots.vo: The logic sounded clever. Phones got better when they lost their buttons. So surely cars would too?
shots.visual: A chunky old mobile with keypad buttons melts into a sleek smartphone; arrow points to a button-covered dashboard melting into a tablet.
shots.anim: Buttons pop off and fly away like popcorn.

shots.vo: And every new model came with more features. Massage seats, ambient lighting, twelve drive modes. There simply wasn't room for a button for everything, so the screen swallowed the lot.
shots.visual: Engineers in a design studio pile labelled toggles (MASSAGE, AMBIENT, DRIVE MODE) onto a crowded dashboard until it overflows; the screen opens like a mouth and gulps them.
shots.anim: Buttons stack, wobble, then get sucked into the screen.

shots.vo: But there's one big problem. A button you can feel. A screen you have to look at. And at seventy miles an hour, there's only one thing your eyes should be looking at. The road.
shots.visual: Close-up on Dave's eyes flicking down to the glow, then up to the road; the windscreen view drifts towards the hard shoulder.
shots.anim: Eye-line arrow flicks down/up; road view drifts; rumble strip buzz.

shots.vo: In 2022, a Swedish car magazine called Vi Bilägare decided to measure exactly how bad this is.
shots.visual: A Swedish test airfield at dawn, pine trees, a line of twelve cars on the runway, a man with a stopwatch and clipboard.
shots.anim: Cars roll into a line; stopwatch glints.

shots.vo: They took twelve cars, drove each one at about seventy miles an hour, and gave the driver four simple jobs. Change the radio, adjust the heating, reset the trip computer, dim the dashboard.
shots.visual: Checklist card with four ticks; a driver in a helmet runs through each task as the car speeds down the runway.
shots.anim: Checklist items tick off one by one.

shots.vo: The winner? A 2005 Volvo V70. Seventeen years old, covered in buttons. All four jobs in ten seconds, about three hundred metres of road.
shots.visual: An old boxy estate on a podium with a winner's rosette; counter: 10 SECONDS · 306 m; nodding dog nods.
shots.anim: Podium rises, rosette pins on, counter counts up fast.

shots.vo: The slowest was the MG Marvel R, an all-screen electric SUV. Forty-five seconds. Nearly one and a half kilometres of road, driven half blind.
shots.visual: A shiny screen-filled SUV; the EYES OFF ROAD meter spins up past 1,400 m; behind it a scale of football pitches laying out end to end.
shots.anim: Meter spins; pitch strips unroll across the frame.

shots.vo: And it gets sillier. In some Teslas, the glovebox opens from a menu on the screen. Even the gears moved there. Swipe up for drive, swipe down for reverse.
shots.visual: Dave in a white saloon tapping the screen to open the glovebox; a gear slider on screen; he swipes the wrong way and the car lurches backwards into a bin.
shots.anim: Swipe gesture, car jolts back, bin wobbles.

shots.vo: Then Volkswagen tried to out-minimal Tesla. It replaced real buttons, even on the steering wheel, with touch-sensitive pads that you could brush by accident.
shots.visual: A German design studio; a designer peels real buttons off a steering wheel and replaces them with shiny touch pads; a driver's thumb brushes one and the volume blasts.
shots.anim: Buttons peeled off; accidental brush triggers a volume blast.

shots.vo: Owners hated it. And in 2025 VW's design boss, Andreas Mindt, said physical buttons were coming back, and promised they would never, ever make that mistake again.
shots.visual: Angry owners with placards; VW design boss at a press conference with a quote card; a box of buttons gets carried back into the studio.
shots.anim: Quote card slams; buttons marched back in.

shots.vo: Mercedes, meanwhile, went the other way. Its MBUX Hyperscreen is glass from pillar to pillar, with a screen just for the passenger.
shots.visual: A glossy motor-show stand, a dashboard that is one wall of glowing glass; the passenger watches cat videos.
shots.anim: Screen lights up pillar to pillar; reflections slide.

shots.vo: Some models even get a dashboard camera for video calls. Yes, you can join the Monday meeting from the driver's seat. And another camera watches your eyes, to check you're not distracted. In a cabin that glows like a nightclub.
shots.visual: Dave in a call grid with colleagues on the dash; a little eye-tracking camera blinks; the whole cabin pulses with purple ambient lighting.
shots.anim: Call tiles pop in; ambient light pulses; camera blinks.

shots.vo: So why push screens so hard? The honest answer is money. A good switch costs real engineering: moving parts, wiring, that lovely solid click. A touchscreen is one part that does everything.
shots.visual: Factory table: on the left a heap of switches, springs and looms with a big price; on the right one flat screen with a small price; an accountant smiles.
shots.anim: Price tags flip; accountant rubs hands.

shots.vo: And once your car has a screen, it can show you anything. Ford has filed a patent for adverts inside the car, based on where you are and where you're going.
shots.visual: A patent document unrolls; Dave drives past a burger place and the dash flashes a cartoon ad with an arrow 'TURN LEFT FOR FRIES'.
shots.anim: Patent unrolls; ad pops onto the dash with a jingle.

shots.vo: Ford says a patent isn't a plan. But some Jeep owners have already reported full-screen pop-up ads at traffic lights. Don't like the ads? I'm sure there'll be an ad-free subscription.
shots.visual: At a red light a pop-up 'EXTENDED WARRANTY!' fills a Jeep-like dash; the driver groans; a little 'GO PREMIUM' button blinks.
shots.anim: Pop-up slides in; driver facepalms; 'GO PREMIUM' blinks.

acts.name: Pay monthly for your own seats

shots.vo: Which brings us to the sneakiest idea of all. Paying a subscription for things your car already has.
shots.visual: A kitchen table at night covered in bills: phone, TV, music, and a new one: CAR SEATS. Dave stares at a banking app.
shots.anim: Bills slide onto the table one by one.

shots.vo: In 2022, BMW owners in Britain found they could pay about fifteen pounds a month to switch on their heated seats. The heaters were already in the seat. You were renting the button.
shots.visual: A seat with glowing heating coils inside, padlocked; a coin slot; Dave feeds £15 and the seat warms; steam rises.
shots.anim: Padlock clicks open as the coin drops.

shots.vo: People were so angry that BMW dropped it a year later. But the idea didn't die.
shots.visual: Angry crowd with pitchforks made of seatbelts; BMW-style exec retreats waving a white flag; a 'subscription' ghost floats away to another showroom.
shots.anim: Flag waves; the ghost drifts off screen.

shots.vo: Mercedes sold extra acceleration on its electric EQS and EQE in America for twelve hundred dollars a year. Same motors, same battery. The power was there all along, locked behind a paywall.
shots.visual: A sleek EV with a speedo needle tied down by a chain and padlock; a key card swipes '$1,200/yr' and the car leaps forward.
shots.anim: Chain snaps, car surges, speed lines.

shots.vo: And when the software stops being supported, the car can lose features you paid for. When America switched off 3G in 2022, early Teslas needed a two-hundred-dollar modem upgrade to stay connected. Some Hondas faced bills of around nine hundred.
shots.visual: A 3G phone mast powers down with sparks; a row of older cars' screens go grey 'NO SIGNAL'; repair invoices flutter down: $200, ~$900.
shots.anim: Mast sparks off; screens fade to grey; invoices fall.

shots.vo: That's the phone business model. Rent you the features, then make the old one feel ancient. The difference is, a phone costs a few hundred pounds. A car costs a lot more.
shots.visual: Dave's old car in a scrapyard next to a pile of old phones; a crane lifts the car onto the phone pile; nodding dog shakes its head.
shots.anim: Crane lift; pile wobbles.

shots.vo: And then, in May 2026, Ferrari showed its first fully electric car, the Luce, in Rome. The interior was designed with Jony Ive's studio. Yes, the man behind the iPhone.
shots.visual: A Rome launch stage at night, columns and spotlights; a veiled car; the cloth slides off; a stylised designer in round glasses gestures calmly at a minimalist cabin.
shots.anim: Cloth slides off; spotlights sweep.

shots.vo: The reaction was brutal. Ferrari's shares fell about eight percent in Milan, billions wiped off in a day. One former Ferrari boss reportedly called it a historic mistake.
shots.visual: Milan stock board, a red line nosediving; traders clutching heads; a quote card 'HISTORIC MISTAKE'.
shots.anim: Line plunges; ticker flashes red.

shots.vo: Enzo Ferrari liked to say he sold engines, and the car came free. The Luce has no engine at all. Somewhere, Enzo is spinning.
shots.visual: Sepia portrait of a stern old man in dark glasses beside a roaring V12 engine; the engine fades; the portrait slowly rotates.
shots.anim: Engine fades to silhouette; portrait spins with a creak.

shots.vo: Porsche learnt the hard way too. After betting big on electric, its operating profit for 2025 fell by about ninety-three percent.
shots.visual: Porsche-style HQ boardroom; a bar chart crumbles from tall to tiny: €5.6bn to €0.4bn; execs stare.
shots.anim: Bars crumble like sandcastles.

shots.vo: And what did Porsche show next? The Mission S concept. A mid-engined supercar with a real key, real buttons, round dials with a proper needle, and no central screen. Need sat nav? There's a holder for your phone.
shots.visual: A warm workshop; dust sheet off a low red concept; close-up: key turned, chunky toggles, an analogue rev needle sweeps; a phone clicks into a little holder; nodding dog nods wildly.
shots.anim: Key turn, needle sweep, phone snaps into holder.

shots.vo: So maybe there's hope. Let carmakers build phones on wheels if they want. But we already have phones. When buyers stop paying for them, watch how fast the buttons come back.
shots.visual: Back on the M62, rain easing to golden dusk; Dave in a car with buttons presses demist by feel; nodding dog nods; EYES OFF ROAD meter resets to 0.
shots.anim: Sun breaks through; meter resets; dog nods.

shots.vo: Would you pay monthly for your own heated seats? Tell me in the comments. And for more stories like this, subscribe to Stormi Explain Everything.
shots.visual: End card space: Stormi mascot beside the nodding dog, comment bubble icon and subscribe button; clean area for end screen.
shots.anim: Comment bubble pops; subscribe bell rings.

hooks: Holding your phone at the wheel is six points and a £200 fine. So why did carmakers bolt a fifteen-inch one to your dashboard?
A 2005 Volvo beat twelve brand-new cars at the simplest test there is: changing the radio at 70 mph.
BMW once charged British drivers fifteen pounds a month to use the heated seats they'd already paid for.
